title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Addiction — August 2026

studies.title: Copying a smoker's body language makes them smoke more — and want to quit less
studies.ns_score_reason: two experiments (one in the wild) showing a purely social, non-pharmacological driver of nicotine consumption; limited by thin reporting of sample details in the abstract.
studies.the_study: Polish researchers ran two experiments on nonverbal mimicry — the unconscious copying of gestures, posture and hand movements that makes people like each other. In a laboratory study, smokers who were subtly mimicked by a confederate smoked more cigarettes, an effect carried by increased liking for the mimicker. In a second, naturalistic study, having their smoking behaviour mimicked reduced smokers' stated desire to quit.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes smoking maintenance as partly a problem of social bonding rather than only of nicotine pharmacology, and suggests the company you smoke in may be as sticky as the drug.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the cigarette break — two people falling into the same posture without noticing, and the finding that this invisible choreography is quietly making both of them smoke more. Hook: "social glue" as a relapse risk. Call Wojciech Kulesza at SWPS University, who has built a career on mimicry effects, and ask what it implies for group-based cessation programmes.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on mimicry as an underexamined lever in all consumption behaviour — drinking rounds, shared vapes, group eating, even sales technique — for a general-interest outlet or a psychology-focused magazine.
studies.caveats: Sample sizes not stated in the abstract; short-term outcomes; laboratory cigarette consumption may not map onto long-term smoking; single research group, no independent replication.

studies.title: People quitting sugar report cravings, low mood and body aches that look like withdrawal
studies.ns_score_reason: applies DSM-5 substance use disorder criteria in real time to sugar quitting, a genuinely contested question; observational and self-reported.
studies.the_study: 203 New Zealand adults who wanted to quit free sugars completed five smartphone surveys a day for two weeks, reporting sugar intake and DSM-5 substance use disorder symptoms. Only 31% stayed sugar-free throughout; the commonest symptoms were craving, preoccupation and difficulty staying abstinent, with withdrawal-like low energy, body aches and low mood. Trajectory modelling split participants into a low-burden (47%) and high-burden (53%) group, with the high group predicted by baseline food-addiction scores, higher BMI, craving, anxiety and stress.
studies.why_it_matters: The "is sugar addictive?" argument has been fought mostly with rodent data and retrospective questionnaires; this puts moment-by-moment human symptom data into it — without settling it.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on someone in the evening slump at 8pm — the peak time participants broke, mostly on desserts and baked goods. The surprise: roughly half of people quitting sugar carry a symptom profile that ticks recognisable substance-withdrawal boxes, and their evening is the danger window. Call Simone Rodda at AUT University on whether "sugar withdrawal" deserves the label.
studies.wider_angle: A sceptic's feature for a health or food-policy outlet on why the food-addiction construct keeps failing to reach diagnostic consensus, and what would actually be needed to prove it — a different story from the symptom-diary one.
studies.caveats: Self-reported intake and symptoms; no pre-quit baseline period, so symptoms cannot be cleanly attributed to abstinence; two-week follow-up only; self-selected motivated quitters; no control group.

studies.title: Brains of people recovering from heroin use fail to sync up when solving problems together
studies.ns_score_reason: first hyperscanning study of social cognition in heroin abstainers, published in a top journal; still modest N and cross-sectional.
studies.the_study: 38 pairs of people with heroin use disorder in abstinence and 30 healthy control pairs did a turn-based group problem-solving task while both partners' brains were recorded simultaneously with functional near-infrared spectroscopy. The heroin group performed worse individually and as pairs, took their partner's perspective less, and showed reduced right inferior frontal gyrus and left orbitofrontal activity — plus disrupted interpersonal neural synchronisation between partners. The behavioural and neural deficits tracked with emotional and sleep-related protracted withdrawal symptoms.
studies.why_it_matters: Addiction research has focused overwhelmingly on solitary reward circuitry; this suggests the damage extends to the machinery of coordinating with another person, which is precisely what recovery — jobs, family, mutual-aid groups — demands.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the image of two brains failing to fall into step. The hook: recovery is usually measured in abstinence days, but this hints at a social deficit that persists into abstinence and could quietly undermine reintegration. Call Hongjun Duan at Shaanxi Normal University.
studies.wider_angle: A trend piece on hyperscanning itself — measuring two or more brains at once — and what "brain-to-brain synchrony" can and cannot tell us, for a neuroscience-literate outlet or a longer feature.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and observational — cannot separate pre-existing traits from drug effects; fNIRS measures only cortical surface activity; participants are abstinent heroin users in one region of China and may not generalise; group sizes modest.

studies.title: Four out of five trading card packs don't tell buyers their odds of a rare card
studies.ns_score_reason: timely audit of a gambling-like product children buy freely; a content analysis rather than a psychology experiment.
studies.the_study: Researchers sampled 50 popular physical card pack products on sale in Hong Kong — trading card games and collectible sports cards — and checked whether the packaging disclosed the probability of getting rare cards. 80% gave no probability information or link at all; the 20% that did were incomplete, sometimes hard to find and occasionally misleading. Not one pack let a buyer work out their odds of any individual card.
studies.why_it_matters: Loot boxes in video games are now regulated or at least scrutinised in several countries; their physical ancestors, bought by children with pocket money, are not — despite evidence linking pack spending to problem gambling.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on a child tearing open a Pokémon pack, or an adult opening a Labubu blind box. The surprise: the digital loot box debate has completely bypassed the cardboard version, which discloses even less. Call Leon Y. Xiao (City University of Hong Kong / BeClaws), the leading academic on loot-box regulation.
studies.wider_angle: A consumer-affairs investigation for a business or consumer outlet on the blind-box economy — Labubu, sneaker drops, mystery boxes — and whether existing consumer law, rather than gambling law, is the enforcement route regulators have overlooked.
studies.caveats: Single jurisdiction (Hong Kong), 50 products; no participant data, so nothing here demonstrates harm — the link to problem gambling comes from other, weaker correlational work.

studies.title: Teenage gambling is falling overall — but rising among gamers and esports fans
studies.ns_score_reason: very large national sample and a genuinely divergent trend, though cross-sectional and self-reported.
studies.the_study: Analysis of 60,331 Spanish adolescents from the nationwide ESTUDES surveys in 2019 and 2021. Gambling with money declined overall across the period, but increased in specific subgroups: video game players (+2.4%), esports spectators (+1.3%) and players (+1.8%), and those with internet gaming disorder (+1.0%). Being male tripled the odds of gambling (OR 3.71); among girls, a new higher-risk profile emerged defined by gaming, esports and internet gaming disorder rather than traditional gambling routes.
studies.why_it_matters: The headline "youth gambling is declining" masks a migration of risk into gaming culture, and the appearance of a female risk profile that existing prevention messaging is not designed for.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the counterintuitive split: the overall curve is going down while the gaming curve goes up. Frame around the girl gamer who is now a demographic that public health hasn't been looking at. Call Pilar Carrasco-Garrido at Universidad Rey Juan Carlos.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a sports or tech outlet on esports and betting — sponsorship, skin gambling, in-stream odds — and how the boundary between competitive gaming and wagering has effectively dissolved for teenagers.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional at two time points, cannot establish causation; self-reported gambling in a school survey; the 2021 wave straddles pandemic disruption, which may confound trends; Spain-specific.

studies.title: Short videos cut depression in older adults through one route and raise it through another
studies.ns_score_reason: large national sample and a nicely opposed dual-pathway result; cross-sectional modelling limits causal claims.
studies.the_study: A national survey of 5,039 Chinese adults aged 50 and over used structural equation modelling to test how short-video use relates to depressive symptoms. Two opposing paths emerged: use predicted *fewer* depressive symptoms via more positive attitudes to ageing, and *more* symptoms via internet addiction. Using more different platforms was associated with higher addiction risk and weaker cognitive benefit; urban and rural patterns diverged.
studies.why_it_matters: It complicates the flat "screens are bad for older people" narrative — the same behaviour appears protective or harmful depending on how it is structured, not how much of it there is.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on a 65-year-old scrolling Douyin. The surprise: the content may be improving how they feel about their own ageing, while the scrolling habit works against them — two effects that partly cancel out in any single-number study. Call Rui Jing at Renmin University of China.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a general-interest or ageing-focused outlet on how older adults are becoming the fastest-growing short-video demographic worldwide, and what platform design aimed at them looks like.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional — the direction of every arrow is assumed, not demonstrated; self-reported depressive symptoms and addiction; Chinese platform ecosystem may not generalise; mediation models of this kind are easy to over-read.

studies.title: Thirteen years of forced addiction treatment: most people relapse, 15% are dead within six months
studies.journal: Australian & New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry
studies.ns_score_reason: the complete record of a rarely used coercive legal power, with stark outcomes; small N and no control group.
studies.the_study: An audit of every admission under Victoria's Severe Substance Dependence Treatment Act from 2011 to 2023 — 70 admissions covering 60 patients. Alcohol was the substance of concern for 91%, 43% had liver disease and 78% had another psychiatric diagnosis. Six months after the end of involuntary treatment, 15% had died and 48% had returned to their previous level of use; 27.6% were abstinent or using less, and early improvement at one month was overwhelmingly predictive of that (OR 70).
studies.why_it_matters: Several jurisdictions are debating expanding involuntary addiction treatment; this is the first full picture of how such a power actually plays out, and the answer is: rarely used, on an extremely sick group, with a minority benefiting.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the number that stops readers: one in seven dead within six months of a treatment imposed to save their life. The honest framing is that this population is desperately unwell rather than that treatment failed. Call Yvonne Bonomo at St Vincent's Hospital Melbourne.
studies.wider_angle: A comparative policy piece for a legal or current-affairs outlet on coercive care across jurisdictions — Sweden, the Netherlands, Canadian provinces, Australian states — and the ethics of detaining someone for their own drug use.
studies.caveats: N=60 patients; no control group, so outcomes cannot be attributed to the treatment; single state, single legal framework; retrospective chart audit; population is at the extreme severity end and not representative of substance use disorders generally.

studies.title: Nearly one in five students shows "maladaptive daydreaming" — and it tracks with ADHD and autism traits
studies.ns_score_reason: a large sample and a reframing of a condition usually filed under dissociation; entirely self-report and cross-sectional.
studies.the_study: 848 Turkish university students (mean age 21.5) completed measures of maladaptive daydreaming, ADHD symptoms, autistic traits, social media and gaming addiction, anxiety, depression, self-esteem, narcissism and loneliness. 18.3% scored above the maladaptive daydreaming cut-off. Low self-esteem, ADHD symptoms and autistic traits were the strongest predictors, with anxiety, social media addiction and narcissistic traits also contributing; severity fell with age and year of study.
studies.why_it_matters: Maladaptive daydreaming — hours lost to immersive, compulsive fantasy — has been theorised mainly as dissociation; this positions it at the intersection of neurodevelopmental traits and behaviourally reinforced habit, which changes who might be looking for it.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on a student who paces their room for two hours a day inside an elaborate imagined life and is late to everything because of it. Hook: this may be less a dissociative curiosity than an under-recognised companion of ADHD and autistic traits. Call Nesrin Serkut Bulut at Marmara University.
studies.wider_angle: A cultural feature for a general-interest magazine on the online communities that named and self-diagnosed maladaptive daydreaming years before psychiatry took it seriously — a case study in patient-led nosology.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional; all measures self-reported, including ADHD and autism traits (no clinical diagnosis); 73% female; single university population; prevalence figure depends entirely on an arbitrary cut-off score.

studies.title: Young people rate nicotine pouches more favourably than vapes or cigarettes
studies.ns_score_reason: first head-to-head comparison of the psychological determinants of three nicotine products in the same young sample; cross-sectional and Finland-specific.
studies.the_study: 1,194 Finnish people aged 15–25 were surveyed on socioeconomic status, health literacy, theory-of-planned-behaviour beliefs, intentions, behaviour and addiction across nicotine vaping, nicotine pouches and cigarettes. Pouches were viewed most favourably of the three, and male gender was more strongly associated with pouch use than with vaping or smoking. Health literacy — but not socioeconomic status — predicted all three behaviours; affective attitudes ("does it feel good?") were the strongest correlate throughout, while instrumental attitudes ("is it useful?") predicted nothing. Friends' norms outweighed family norms, especially for smoking.
studies.why_it_matters: Nicotine pouches are the fastest-moving new nicotine product in Europe and this suggests prevention aimed at facts and consequences is targeting exactly the wrong kind of attitude.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the finding that rational arguments — instrumental attitudes — had zero predictive power, while gut feeling had the most. Frame around a 17-year-old with a pouch under their lip who knows all the health information and uses it anyway. Call Kyra Hamilton or Martin Hagger.
studies.wider_angle: A public-health and industry piece for a policy or business outlet on how nicotine pouches slipped into a regulatory gap across Europe, and how they are marketed — especially to young men.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and self-reported, including addiction; single country with an unusual nicotine market (Nordic snus culture); wide age band 15–25; cannot establish causation.

studies.title: Trying harder to self-regulate makes short-video addiction worse — for some people
studies.ns_score_reason: a "backfire effect" for self-control strategies is a strong hook, but it rests on cross-sectional moderated mediation.
studies.the_study: Using focus groups with 169 addicted and non-addicted short-video users to define constructs, then a survey of 1,274 people, researchers tested a moderated mediation model within the I-PACE framework. Among people with low inhibitory control, greater use of self-regulatory strategies was associated with *higher* addiction severity — a possible backfire effect — while among those with high inhibitory control such strategies were largely redundant. Pathways also differed by group: addicted users were driven mainly by pursuit of positive emotion, non-addicted users by self-regulation acting as a defence.
studies.why_it_matters: If confirmed prospectively, it would suggest that the standard advice — set limits, monitor yourself, use screen-time tools — may be counterproductive for precisely the people who most need help.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on someone who has installed four app blockers and is scrolling more than ever. Hook: self-control advice may need to be triaged by whether the person has the inhibitory capacity to act on it. Be explicit that this is correlational. Call Xin Li at Shanghai Polytechnic University.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a technology outlet on the screen-time-tools industry — Screen Time, Digital Wellbeing, blocker apps — and the thinness of the evidence that any of them work.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and self-reported; the "backfire" is equally consistent with reverse causation (people who are struggling most try the most strategies); Chinese sample; no clinical diagnosis of addiction.

studies.title: Most teenagers who self-harm stop within two years — and for boys, cutting internet use tracks with stopping
studies.ns_score_reason: genuinely longitudinal with good retention and a striking remission rate; single-city sample and wide confidence intervals.
studies.the_study: 652 first-year junior high students in Jingzhou, China were surveyed in 2021 and 585 (89.7%) followed up in 2023. Non-suicidal self-injury fell from 22.1% to 8.6%, with 82.2% of those affected at baseline having stopped. Remission was strongly predicted by falling depressive symptoms (aOR 8.43) and stable rather than worsening anxiety. Gender-stratified analysis found that among boys a reduction in internet addiction predicted remission (aOR 8.87), while among girls the depression and anxiety pathways dominated.
studies.why_it_matters: The dominant public narrative is of relentlessly rising adolescent self-harm; this shows high natural remission over two years, and points to different mechanisms in boys and girls.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the remission figure — four in five stopped — as a counterweight to catastrophising coverage, then the gender split in what accompanied stopping. Frame around the two-year window between ages 12 and 14. Call Xiaoping Deng at Yangtze University.
studies.wider_angle: A methodological feature for a science or health outlet on why cross-sectional prevalence snapshots systematically mislead about adolescent mental health, and what cohort data show instead.
studies.caveats: Two schools in one Chinese city; self-reported self-harm and internet addiction; very wide confidence intervals on the gender-stratified odds ratios; observational — reduced internet use may be a marker of recovery rather than a cause; follow-up spans a period of pandemic disruption.

studies.title: Women who smoke are twice as likely to develop postpartum depression
studies.ns_score_reason: a clear meta-analytic effect across 38 studies with a timing moderator; the bolt-on in silico genomics adds little and the design cannot address causation.
studies.the_study: A meta-analysis of 38 primary epidemiological studies found that women who smoke are roughly twice as likely as non-smokers to develop postpartum depression, with higher depression scores overall. Timing mattered: current and gestational smoking were more strongly linked to PPD than past smoking, while geographical and cultural setting did not moderate the effect. A companion network analysis identified shared hub genes between nicotine addiction and PPD pathways (including IL6, TNF, IL1B, AKT1, ESR1).
studies.why_it_matters: It sharpens a link that previous reviews called inconclusive and makes smoking status during pregnancy a candidate flag for postpartum depression risk — though nothing here shows that quitting reduces that risk.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the timing moderator: it is current and pregnancy smoking, not a smoking history, that carries the association — which points away from "smokers are just different people" and towards something active. Do not imply that quitting prevents PPD. Call Faraz Ahmad at Vellore Institute of Technology.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a health or women's-health outlet on how much maternal mental health research still treats smoking as a nuisance covariate to adjust away rather than a variable worth studying.
studies.caveats: Meta-analysis of observational studies — confounding by socioeconomic status, prior depression and stress is very likely; heterogeneity across 38 studies not detailed in the abstract; the genomics component is purely computational with no experimental validation.

studies.title: Severe social withdrawal explains the link between autistic traits and problem gaming
studies.ns_score_reason: first study to test all three constructs together in a large sample; cross-sectional mediation cannot establish the sequence it implies.
studies.the_study: 2,168 Italian university students completed measures of internet and computer game addiction, subthreshold autistic traits and hikikomori-style social withdrawal. Students classified as pathological gamers scored higher on both autistic traits and hikikomori tendencies, and mediation analysis found that withdrawal partly explained the route from autistic traits to gaming addiction, hours played and gaming-related academic problems.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that gaming may sit downstream of withdrawal rather than causing it in this group — with implications for whether you treat the gaming or the retreat from social life.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the reversal of the usual causal story parents assume: the gaming may be the symptom, not the cause, in young people with high autistic traits. Note honestly that a cross-sectional design cannot prove the ordering. Call Barbara Carpita or Liliana Dell'Osso at the University of Pisa.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a general-interest outlet on hikikomori going global — how a phenomenon first named in Japan is now being measured in Italian universities, and whether the concept survives export.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional, so the mediation direction is assumed; all self-report, including autistic traits (subthreshold, not diagnosed); university students only; single-country sample.

studies.title: People with cocaine use disorder have two separate kinds of impulsivity — with different brain wiring
studies.ns_score_reason: challenges the treatment of impulsivity as one thing, but the abstract omits sample size and the material is technical for a 600-word piece.
studies.the_study: Combining self-report measures, clinical assessment and behavioural tasks with structural connectome modelling, researchers found that disinhibition in cocaine use disorder splits into two partially separable dimensions — trait disinhibition and cognitive disinhibition. These map onto largely distinct structural connectivity signatures, sharing only a single overlapping connection between the left amygdala and right medial prefrontal cortex. Cognitive disinhibition involved widely distributed connectivity across visual, somatomotor, default mode and subcortical networks; trait disinhibition involved reduced somatomotor–control connectivity and increased nodal clustering.
studies.why_it_matters: If "impulsivity" in addiction is at least two things with different wiring, then measuring it with one questionnaire — as most studies do — is averaging over a real distinction.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the near-total non-overlap: one shared connection between two things psychiatry calls by the same name. Frame around the person who is impulsive on a lab task but not in life, or vice versa. Call Yuanyuan Wang at Jinan University.
studies.wider_angle: A specialist piece for a neuroscience or psychiatry outlet on connectome-based predictive modelling and the transdiagnostic push to replace diagnostic labels with measurable dimensions.
studies.caveats: Sample size not stated in the abstract; cross-sectional; connectome-based predictive models frequently fail to replicate in independent samples; single site; cannot separate cause from consequence of cocaine use.

studies.title: Anxious ultramarathon runners get injured more — and for women, a lot more
studies.ns_score_reason: an unexpected psychological predictor of physical injury in an extreme-endurance group; cross-sectional, self-reported, wide confidence intervals.
studies.the_study: 495 Brazilian ultramarathon runners (mean age 44.5) completed an online survey covering training parameters, injury history, generalised anxiety and exercise addiction. Injury prevalence was 27.7%. Higher BMI, low-level anxiety (OR 1.62) and severe anxiety (OR 3.26) were all associated with injury; among women, severe anxiety carried a very large but imprecisely estimated association with injury (OR 15.92, CI 2.47–102.31), while among men only low-level anxiety reached significance.
studies.why_it_matters: Sports medicine models injury from load, biomechanics and recovery; this adds mental state as a candidate variable, and suggests the addiction-adjacent psychology of extreme endurance deserves proper study.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on an ultrarunner strapping up an old injury for another 100km. Hook: the strongest predictor in the data wasn't weekly mileage, it was anxiety. Be careful — recall bias could produce this pattern in reverse. Call Mabliny Thuany at State University of Pará or Volker Scheer at the Ultra Sports Science Foundation.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a sports or general-interest outlet on exercise addiction as the one compulsion society still applauds, and where endurance-sport culture draws the line between dedication and disorder.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional web survey with self-selected respondents; injury and anxiety both self-reported and retrospective (injured runners may recall or report more anxiety); the female severe-anxiety confidence interval spans nearly two orders of magnitude; exercise addiction measured but not reported as a predictor.

studies.title: Exercise addiction and eating disorders look similar but come from different emotional places
studies.ns_score_reason: a useful dissociation between two co-occurring syndromes, but cross-sectional, sample size unreported and the authors themselves flag it as preliminary.
studies.the_study: A community sample of recreational exercisers completed measures of eating-disorder symptoms, exercise addiction symptoms, adult attachment anxiety and avoidance, and emotion-regulation difficulties. Both symptom sets were correlated, but showed partly different profiles: eating-disorder symptoms aligned more with attachment anxiety and a lack of emotional awareness, while exercise addiction symptoms aligned more with attachment *avoidance* and non-acceptance of one's own emotions.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests compulsive exercise is not simply an eating disorder wearing trainers — the emotional strategy behind it (avoidant self-reliance, control through movement) may be distinct, which matters for how it is recognised.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the distinction: one pattern is about not noticing your feelings, the other about refusing to accept them. Open on a gym regular whose training is a way of not sitting with distress. Call Dalit Lev Arey at the Academic College of Tel Aviv Yaffo.
studies.wider_angle: A piece for a fitness or lifestyle outlet on the wellness industry's blind spot — how "discipline" branding rewards exactly the avoidant regulatory pattern described here.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional; sample size not stated in the abstract; community volunteers, not a clinical sample; all self-report; authors describe path analyses as exploratory and call for replication.

studies.title: "Love addiction" is linked to distress and impulsivity — but only through a loss of emotional control
studies.ns_score_reason: a relatable construct with a specific, gender-invariant mechanism; cross-sectional self-report on a contested diagnostic category.
studies.the_study: 714 participants (mean age 26, 68% women) completed measures of psychological distress, motor impulsivity, emotion-regulation difficulties and love addiction. Both distress and impulsivity were directly associated with love addiction, and both were also indirectly associated with it through one specific pathway only — lack of emotional control — with the distress route the stronger of the two. Multigroup analysis showed the model was strictly invariant across genders.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives a testable mechanism to a folk concept, and the gender invariance undercuts the stereotype that compulsive romantic attachment is a distinctively female pattern.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on someone who can't stop checking whether their partner has read the message. Hook: the same model fits men and women identically, and the active ingredient is losing control of emotions rather than distress itself. Call María Sánchez-Fernández at the University of Cadiz — and ask her directly whether "love addiction" should be a clinical category at all.
studies.wider_angle: A sceptical feature for a general-interest outlet on the proliferation of behavioural addictions — love, shopping, exercise, work — and the debate over whether the addiction framework is being stretched past usefulness.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional, so mediation direction is assumed; all self-report; "love addiction" is not a recognised diagnosis and the measure's validity is contested; Spanish sample skewed female and young.

studies.title: Employees who use generative AI think more creatively — until tolerance sets in
studies.ns_score_reason: extremely topical framing of AI dependence, but a small cross-sectional survey with self-reported everything.
studies.the_study: 194 Chinese knowledge workers were surveyed on generative AI use, creative self-efficacy, AI addiction (tolerance and withdrawal dimensions) and creative thinking. AI use was positively associated with creative thinking, mediated by creative self-efficacy — but the *tolerance* dimension of AI addiction was negatively associated with creative thinking, while withdrawal was not. Creative self-efficacy also negatively predicted both addiction dimensions, and satisfaction with AI use strengthened the positive path.
studies.why_it_matters: Not much yet, but it opens a line of enquiry: whether escalating reliance on generative AI — needing more of it to feel the same benefit — erodes the very capability it initially boosts.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the split result: the same tool appears to help and hinder the same skill, depending on whether the person has developed tolerance to it. Open on a designer who now can't start a brief without a prompt. Flag the design limits prominently. Call Wenping Zhang at Anhui University of Technology.
studies.wider_angle: A workplace feature for a business or technology outlet on "AI deskilling" — the emerging evidence on cognitive offloading and whether organisations should be measuring dependence alongside productivity.
studies.caveats: N=194, cross-sectional, single country, all self-reported including creativity; "GAI addiction" is a newly minted construct with no established validity; no objective measure of creative output; effects could easily run in the opposite direction.

studies.title: Across 15 countries, conflict with others is the hub connecting internet addiction to teen mental health
studies.ns_score_reason: a big, geographically underrepresented sample and a specific symptom-level target; network analyses of cross-sectional data are descriptive.
studies.the_study: 6,204 young people aged 15–24 across 15 Eastern Mediterranean countries completed the Compulsive Internet Use Scale and the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire between June and December 2024. In gender-stratified network models, "conflict" was the most central internet-addiction domain in both sexes, and "nervous in new situations" the most influential psychological symptom. The strongest cross-domain bridge was internet-related withdrawal; at item level, preferring online engagement to being with others linked most strongly to solitary behaviour.
studies.why_it_matters: Most internet-addiction network research comes from East Asia and Europe; this fills a large regional gap and converges on interpersonal conflict rather than time online as the connective tissue.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is that the symptom binding compulsive internet use to distress is not hours or craving but conflict with the people around you. Frame around a household argument. Call Noha Fadl at Alexandria University.
studies.wider_angle: A global-health piece for a development or international-affairs outlet on how digital mental health research is geographically skewed, and what changes when the same instruments are run in the Middle East and North Africa.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and observational; recruitment method across 15 countries unclear from the abstract and likely convenience-based online sampling; all self-report; network centrality does not identify causes or intervention targets despite being routinely described that way.

citation_table.journal: Australian & New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry

trends_raw: _No prior digest on this topic to compare against yet — this is the first run._
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** A large share of this batch treats addiction as something that happens *between* people rather than inside a reward circuit — and keeps finding that the interpersonal signal is the strongest one. Mimicking a smoker's body language makes them smoke more and want to quit less (PMID 42427246); recovering heroin users' brains fail to synchronise with a partner during joint problem-solving, with deficits tracking protracted withdrawal (PMID 41941931); across 15 Eastern Mediterranean countries, "conflict with others" — not hours online or craving — is the central hub linking compulsive internet use to adolescent distress (PMID 42612478); hikikomori-style social withdrawal mediates the route from autistic traits to problem gaming (PMID 41742036); and among Finnish 15–25s, friends' norms outweigh family norms and gut-level affective attitudes predict nicotine pouch use while rational "is it useful?" beliefs predict nothing at all (PMID 42581660). Exercise addiction's alignment with attachment *avoidance* rather than anxiety (PMID 42504448) and love addiction's routing through loss of emotional control (PMID 42533520) extend the same theme into the relational dimension of behavioural compulsions.

**Why pitch this now:** Addiction coverage and addiction policy are both still organised around the solitary brain — dopamine, craving, abstinence day counts — while a cluster of 2026 studies using new tools (dual-brain hyperscanning, symptom network models, naturalistic mimicry experiments) is independently converging on social bonds, conflict and withdrawal from others as the load-bearing variables, which points at completely different intervention targets.

**Angle:** "The social brain of addiction": a feature arguing that the field's neurocentric, individual-level model is measuring the wrong unit of analysis — following two brains in a scanner, a cigarette break, and a household argument to ask what treatment would look like if the target were the relationship rather than the receptor. Best for a neuroscience-literate general readership that has already absorbed the "addiction is a brain disease" framing and is ready to hear it complicated.

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — the Mind section has the room to run the hyperscanning imagery alongside the mimicry experiment, and the "your brain isn't the unit of addiction" reframe is exactly its house contrarian-but-evidenced register.
- **BBC Future** — strong fit for a long explanatory piece on social contagion of everyday behaviours (cigarette breaks, drinking rounds, shared vapes), with the mimicry study as a concrete, reproducible hook.
- **Knowable Magazine** — built for "here's how a field is quietly changing its model," and could carry the methodological throughline of hyperscanning and symptom-network analysis without dumbing it down.
- **Undark** — would take the policy sting: if conflict and social reintegration are the active ingredients, abstinence-counting and coercive treatment regimes (PMID 42017394) are aimed at the wrong outcome.

# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Addiction — August 2026
**Checked:** 2026-08-24 | **Studies reviewed:** 19
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run date 2026-08-24

---

### Study 1: Copying a smoker's body language makes them smoke more — and want to quit less
**PMID:** 42427246 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Confederate" detail not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "smokers who were subtly mimicked by a confederate smoked more cigarettes"
- **Abstract says:** "A first laboratory experiment showed that nonverbal mimicry (physical actions, hand and arm movements and body posture) increases cigarette consumption due to increased liking for the mimicker."
- **Problem:** The abstract never specifies who did the mimicking or that it was covert. It is the standard paradigm, but it is an assumption at this stage. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "smokers who were mimicked during the interaction smoked more cigarettes, an effect carried by increased liking for the mimicker (the abstract does not describe who performed the mimicry)."

**Issue B. NS fit score of 7 with no reported sample sizes** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "NS fit: 7/10 — two experiments (one in the wild) showing a purely social, non-pharmacological driver of nicotine consumption; limited by thin reporting of sample details in the abstract."
- **Abstract says:** No N reported for either experiment.
- **Problem:** A 7 implies solid evidential footing, but neither experiment's size, randomisation nor effect magnitude can be checked from the abstract. The score is being carried by the design in principle rather than by verifiable numbers.
- **Suggested fix:** "NS fit: 6/10 — pending sight of the full text; two experiments with unreported sample sizes and effect sizes."

---

### Study 2: People quitting sugar report cravings, low mood and body aches that look like withdrawal
**PMID:** 41905576 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues (one Moderate)

**Issue A. High-burden group described as a withdrawal profile** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "roughly half of people quitting sugar carry a symptom profile that ticks recognisable substance-withdrawal boxes"
- **Abstract says:** "Group-based trajectory modelling identified a low (47%) and high (53%) symptom burden group." The most frequent symptoms overall were "cravings, preoccupation and difficulty remaining abstinent" — i.e. impaired-control criteria, not withdrawal.
- **Problem:** The 53% group is defined by overall DSM-5 SUD symptom burden across five criterion clusters, not by a withdrawal syndrome. The pitch converts a broad symptom-burden trajectory into a specific withdrawal claim, which is the more exciting but unsupported reading.
- **Suggested fix:** "roughly half of participants fell into a high symptom-burden group, reporting DSM-5-style symptoms — mostly craving, preoccupation and difficulty staying abstinent, with some withdrawal-like low energy, aches and low mood."

**Issue B. Invented clock time** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the evening slump at 8pm — the peak time participants broke"
- **Abstract says:** "Sugar consumption was reported in 9% of EMAs and peaked in the evening EMA (11.5%), primarily as snacks and desserts or baked goods."
- **Problem:** The abstract says "the evening EMA", not 8pm. The survey schedule is not given.
- **Suggested fix:** "the evening survey window — when sugar consumption peaked — mostly on snacks, desserts and baked goods."

**Issue C. Two predictors of high-burden group membership dropped** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the high group predicted by baseline food-addiction scores, higher BMI, craving, anxiety and stress"
- **Abstract says:** "...presence of food addiction as per Yale Food Addiction Scale, higher sugar consumption, BMI, craving, anxiety, and stress, as well as lower self-efficacy."
- **Problem:** Higher baseline sugar consumption and lower self-efficacy are omitted; also "associated with" in the abstract becomes "predicted by".
- **Suggested fix:** "high-burden membership was associated with baseline food-addiction scores, higher baseline sugar intake, higher BMI, craving, anxiety, stress and lower self-efficacy."

**Issue D. NS fit 7 on fully self-reported, uncontrolled data** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "NS fit: 7/10"
- **Problem:** Every outcome is self-reported via smartphone, there is no control group and no pre-quit baseline (the digest's own caveats concede this). A 7 overstates the evidential weight on a contested question.
- **Suggested fix:** "NS fit: 6/10 — novel real-time data on a contested question, but self-reported, uncontrolled and without a pre-quit baseline."

---

### Study 3: Brains of people recovering from heroin use fail to sync up when solving problems together
**PMID:** 41941931 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "First hyperscanning study" claim not made in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Novelty: First-in-class … first hyperscanning study of social cognition in heroin abstainers"
- **Abstract says:** "Despite extensive research on the neurobiology of addiction, little is known about how repeated drug use and withdrawal are related to social functioning impairments in humans."
- **Problem:** The authors claim novelty of insight, not priority. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "an early — possibly the first — hyperscanning study of social cognition in heroin abstainers (priority claim to be confirmed with the authors)."

**Issue B. Participant location stated but not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "participants are abstinent heroin users in one region of China"
- **Abstract says:** Author affiliations are in Xi'an, China; participant recruitment location is not stated.
- **Problem:** Reasonable inference, but presented as fact. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "participants were recruited by a Chinese research group (recruitment site not specified in the abstract)."

---

### Study 4: Four out of five trading card packs don't tell buyers their odds of a rare card
**PMID:** 42611551 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Significant-adjacent (Moderate)

**Issue A. "Any individual card" reverses the scope of the finding** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Not one pack let a buyer work out their odds of any individual card."
- **Abstract says:** "No pack (0.0%) allowed the consumer to know their odds of getting every individual card."
- **Problem:** "Every" and "any" are not interchangeable here. The study found no pack gave complete card-by-card odds; the digest's wording claims no pack gave odds for even a single card, which is contradicted by the 20% that provided (incomplete) disclosures.
- **Suggested fix:** "No pack gave complete odds — none let a buyer work out their chance of getting every individual card."

---

### Study 5: Teenage gambling is falling overall — but rising among gamers and esports fans
**PMID:** 42599567 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Tripled" understates the reported odds ratio** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Being male tripled the odds of gambling (OR 3.71)"
- **Abstract says:** "males compared to females (OR 3.71, 95%CI 3.39-4.06)"
- **Problem:** 3.71 is closer to quadruple than triple; "tripled" also reads as causal for a cross-sectional association.
- **Suggested fix:** "Boys had nearly four times the odds of gambling as girls (OR 3.71, 95% CI 3.39–4.06)."

**Issue B. "Rather than traditional gambling routes" is an addition** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "among girls, a new higher-risk profile emerged defined by gaming, esports and internet gaming disorder rather than traditional gambling routes"
- **Abstract says:** "In female adolescents, the new profile with a higher likelihood of gambling includes videogame players, esport spectator and/or player, and presence of internet gaming disorders."
- **Problem:** The abstract describes an additional profile; it does not report that traditional routes have been displaced in girls.
- **Suggested fix:** "…a newly identified higher-risk profile among girls: video game players, esports spectators and players, and those with internet gaming disorder."

---

### Study 6: Short videos cut depression in older adults through one route and raise it through another
**PMID:** 42374855 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Moderate issue

**Issue A. Causal headline on a cross-sectional SEM** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Short videos cut depression in older adults through one route and raise it through another"
- **Abstract says:** "Short video use was associated with fewer depressive symptoms via more positive attitudes toward aging, but also with increased symptoms via Internet addiction."
- **Problem:** "Cut" and "raise" assert causation from a single-wave national survey with modelled pathways. The digest's own caveat concedes "the direction of every arrow is assumed" — the headline contradicts it.
- **Suggested fix:** "Short video use is linked to less depression in older adults by one route — and more by another."

---

### Study 7: Thirteen years of forced addiction treatment: most people relapse, 15% are dead within six months
**PMID:** 42017394 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Moderate issue

**Issue A. "Most people relapse" is not supported by 48%** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "most people relapse, 15% are dead within six months"
- **Abstract says:** "Six months after the end of treatment, 15% were deceased and 48% of patients had returned to their previous level of substance use. 27.6% were either using less or abstinent at 6 months."
- **Problem:** 48% is not "most". The headline claims a majority relapsed when the study reports just under half returning to previous levels, with a further quarter improved and 15% deceased.
- **Suggested fix:** "Thirteen years of involuntary addiction treatment: nearly half return to previous use, 15% are dead within six months."

**Issue B. "The" vs "a" substance of concern** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Alcohol was the substance of concern for 91%"
- **Abstract says:** "Alcohol was a substance of concern for 91%."
- **Problem:** The abstract allows for polysubstance presentations; "the" implies alcohol was the sole concern.
- **Suggested fix:** "Alcohol was a substance of concern for 91%."

---

### Study 8: Nearly one in five students shows "maladaptive daydreaming" — and it tracks with ADHD and autism traits
**PMID:** 42102505 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N (848), mean age (21.50), prevalence (18.3% at MDS-16 ≥50), the strongest regression predictors, the secondary contributors and the inverse associations with age and year of study all match. Framing is correlational throughout and the caveats (self-report, 73% female, cut-off dependence) match the abstract. NS fit of 6 is defensible.

---

### Study 9: Young people rate nicotine pouches more favourably than vapes or cigarettes
**PMID:** 42581660 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issue

**Issue A. Market claim not supported by the study** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Nicotine pouches are the fastest-moving new nicotine product in Europe"
- **Abstract says:** "Youth vaping and nicotine pouch use have risen as cigarette smoking declines, yet comparative evidence on their determinants remains limited."
- **Problem:** The "fastest-moving in Europe" claim comes from outside the paper and needs an independent source before it goes in a pitch. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Nicotine pouch use is rising among young people as smoking declines [source needed], and this suggests prevention aimed at facts and consequences targets the wrong kind of attitude."

Otherwise all figures (N=1,194; ages 15–25; health literacy but not SES predicting all three; affective attitudes strongest; instrumental attitudes null; friend norms > family norms) match the abstract exactly.

---

### Study 10: Trying harder to self-regulate makes short-video addiction worse — for some people
**PMID:** 42374874 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Moderate issue

**Issue A. Causal headline contradicts the body's own hedge** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Trying harder to self-regulate makes short-video addiction worse — for some people"
- **Abstract says:** "For individuals with low inhibitory control, greater use of self-regulatory strategies was associated with higher addiction severity, suggesting a conditional risk pattern consistent with a possible 'backfire effect.'"
- **Problem:** "Makes … worse" asserts causation from cross-sectional moderated mediation. The digest's pitch instructs "be explicit that this is correlational" — the headline does the opposite, and the caveat notes reverse causation is equally consistent.
- **Suggested fix:** "In people with low inhibitory control, more self-regulation strategies go with worse short-video addiction, not better."

**Issue B. Focus groups described as a separate stage** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "focus groups with 169 addicted and non-addicted short-video users to define constructs, then a survey of 1,274 people"
- **Abstract says:** "...core affective and cognitive variables first defined through focus groups with a strategically selected subsample (N = 169) of addicted and nonaddicted users."
- **Problem:** The 169 were a subsample of the survey participants, not an independent prior sample.
- **Suggested fix:** "a survey of 1,274 people, with constructs first defined through focus groups with a strategically selected subsample of 169 of them."

---

### Study 11: Most teenagers who self-harm stop within two years — and for boys, cutting internet use tracks with stopping
**PMID:** 42633531 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Baseline N (652), follow-up N and rate (585, 89.7%), NSSI prevalence change (22.05%→8.55%), remission rate (82.17%), aOR 8.43 for reduced depressive symptoms, aOR 8.87 for reduced internet addiction in boys, and the girls' depression/anxiety pathways all match. The headline correctly uses "tracks with" rather than causal language, and the caveats on wide CIs and reverse causation are appropriate. NS fit of 5 is defensible.

---

### Study 12: Women who smoke are twice as likely to develop postpartum depression
**PMID:** 42604887 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline states an observational association as a fact about risk** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Women who smoke are twice as likely to develop postpartum depression"
- **Abstract says:** "Meta-analytical assessment of systematically collected data from 38 studies indicated that smoking women are twice as likely to develop PPD, compared to their non-smoking counterparts… although this association involve mediation of additional environmental and psychosocial elements."
- **Problem:** The headline mirrors the abstract's phrasing, but strips the authors' own acknowledgement of confounding. On a topic where readers will hear "smoking causes PPD", a hedge is worth carrying into the headline.
- **Suggested fix:** "Smoking is linked to double the rate of postpartum depression across 38 studies."

**Issue B. "New mechanism" novelty tag for an in silico analysis** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Novelty: New mechanism"
- **Abstract says:** The gene-level work is "in silico analyses" of "common protein-encoding genes… predicted to alter multiple pathophysiological pathways."
- **Problem:** Nothing mechanistic was demonstrated; hub genes were computationally predicted. The digest's caveats say as much, but the novelty label oversells it.
- **Suggested fix:** "Novelty: Consolidates a contested association (mechanistic component is computational only)."

---

### Study 13: Severe social withdrawal explains the link between autistic traits and problem gaming
**PMID:** 41742036 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Moderate issue

**Issue A. Mediation extended to outcomes it wasn't tested on** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "mediation analysis found that withdrawal partly explained the route from autistic traits to gaming addiction, hours played and gaming-related academic problems"
- **Abstract says:** "AdAS Spectrum and HQ-25 total scores… emerged as significant positive predictors of AICA-S total score, of a greater number of hours spent playing video games and of the presence of school-related issues… A mediation analysis demonstrated significant direct and indirect effect through the HQ-25, of the AdAS Spectrum total score on the AICA-S total score."
- **Problem:** The mediation was tested only on the AICA-S total score. Hours played and school-related issues come from a separate regression in which both constructs were predictors — not from the mediation model.
- **Suggested fix:** "Mediation analysis found withdrawal partly explained the route from autistic traits to gaming-addiction scores; both autistic traits and withdrawal separately predicted hours played and gaming-related school problems."

**Issue B. Headline "explains" is stronger than partial mediation** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Severe social withdrawal explains the link between autistic traits and problem gaming"
- **Abstract says:** "significant direct and indirect effect through the HQ-25" — i.e. partial, not full, mediation, in cross-sectional data.
- **Problem:** "Explains" implies the link is accounted for; a direct effect remained.
- **Suggested fix:** "Social withdrawal partly accounts for the link between autistic traits and problem gaming."

---

### Study 14: People with cocaine use disorder have two separate kinds of impulsivity — with different brain wiring
**PMID:** 42562118 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Overturns prior research" is the wrong novelty label** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Novelty: Overturns prior research"
- **Abstract says:** "However, accumulating evidence suggests that disinhibition comprises multiple partially dissociable dimensions. It remains unclear how these dimensions manifest in CUD."
- **Problem:** The multidimensional view is already established in the literature; this study extends it to CUD and to structural connectomes. It does not overturn anything.
- **Suggested fix:** "Novelty: Extends an existing dimensional framework to cocaine use disorder."

**Issue B. "Two separate kinds" overstates "partially dissociable"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** Headline: "have two separate kinds of impulsivity"
- **Abstract says:** "two partially dissociable dimensions… partially overlapping but largely separable structural connectome architectures."
- **Problem:** The body text correctly says "partially separable"; the headline hardens it to fully separate.
- **Suggested fix:** "Cocaine use disorder involves two largely separable kinds of impulsivity — with different brain wiring."

---

### Study 15: Anxious ultramarathon runners get injured more — and for women, a lot more
**PMID:** 42628162 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Strongest predictor wasn't weekly mileage" is not established** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the strongest predictor in the data wasn't weekly mileage, it was anxiety"
- **Abstract says:** Reports only that "Age, BMI, and generalized anxiety disorder were significantly associated with injury risk"; training parameters were collected but no result for weekly mileage is given.
- **Problem:** The absence of training variables from the reported results is not the same as a demonstrated null, and no head-to-head comparison of effect strength is reported. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "the variables that came out significant were BMI, age and anxiety — training volume did not feature in the reported results."

**Issue B. Causal headline on a retrospective self-report survey** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Anxious ultramarathon runners get injured more"
- **Abstract says:** Cross-sectional web survey; "self-reported injury history"; GAD "associated with injury".
- **Problem:** "Get injured more" implies a prospective relationship; injury history was recalled at the same moment anxiety was measured, and the digest's own caveat raises recall bias.
- **Suggested fix:** "Ultramarathon runners with anxiety report more injuries — and for women, far more."

---

### Study 16: Exercise addiction and eating disorders look similar but come from different emotional places
**PMID:** 42504448 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issue

**Issue A. "Come from" implies origin from cross-sectional correlations** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Exercise addiction and eating disorders look similar but come from different emotional places"
- **Abstract says:** "The findings provide preliminary support for partially differentiated psychological patterns… These cross-sectional findings should be interpreted cautiously and require replication in longitudinal and clinical samples."
- **Problem:** "Come from" asserts an origin story the design cannot support; the authors explicitly label the result preliminary and partial. The body text ("partly different profiles") is fine.
- **Suggested fix:** "Exercise addiction and eating disorders look similar but map onto different emotional patterns."

---

### Study 17: "Love addiction" is linked to distress and impulsivity — but only through a loss of emotional control
**PMID:** 42533520 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Moderate issue

**Issue A. Gender invariance misread as evidence against a gender stereotype** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "the gender invariance undercuts the stereotype that compulsive romantic attachment is a distinctively female pattern"
- **Abstract says:** "multigroup analysis confirmed that the structural model was strictly invariant across genders."
- **Problem:** Structural invariance means the *pathways between constructs* operate the same way in men and women. It says nothing about whether men and women report equivalent *levels* of love addiction — which is what the stereotype is about. The digest's pitch angle repeats the misreading ("the same model fits men and women identically" is fine; the stereotype claim is not).
- **Suggested fix:** "the model works identically in men and women, meaning the mechanism is not gender-specific — though the study does not report whether levels of love addiction differ by gender."

**Issue B. Sample nationality asserted** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Spanish sample skewed female and young"
- **Abstract says:** Authors are based at Cadiz and Seville; participant nationality is not stated.
- **Problem:** Reasonable inference, but not in the abstract. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Sample skewed female and young; recruitment country not specified in the abstract (authors are Spain-based)."

---

### Study 18: Employees who use generative AI think more creatively — until tolerance sets in
**PMID:** 42364395 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Moderate issue

**Issue A. Headline implies a temporal progression not tested** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Employees who use generative AI think more creatively — until tolerance sets in"
- **Abstract says:** "A cross-sectional questionnaire survey was conducted among 194 knowledge workers… GAI use is positively associated with employee creative thinking… the tolerance dimension of GAI addiction is negatively associated with creative thinking."
- **Problem:** "Until tolerance sets in" describes a within-person trajectory over time. This is a single-timepoint survey of 194 people; two opposing cross-sectional associations were found simultaneously, not sequentially. The "Why it matters" section is appropriately hedged, so the headline is the outlier.
- **Suggested fix:** "Generative AI use goes with more creative thinking — but signs of tolerance go with less."

Other figures (N=194, mediation via creative self-efficacy, null withdrawal pathway, self-efficacy negatively predicting both addiction dimensions, satisfaction as moderator of the use→self-efficacy path) all check out.

---

### Study 19: Across 15 countries, conflict with others is the hub connecting internet addiction to teen mental health
**PMID:** 42612478 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Moderate issue

**Issue A. Central node conflated with the connecting bridge** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** Headline: "conflict with others is the hub connecting internet addiction to teen mental health"; and "converges on interpersonal conflict rather than time online as the connective tissue"
- **Abstract says:** "the domain-level analysis identified conflict as the most central domain… Internet-related withdrawal formed the strongest cross-domain associations with psychological problems."
- **Problem:** Conflict was the most central node *within* the network; the strongest *bridge* between internet addiction and psychological problems was withdrawal. The headline and "Why it matters" assign the bridging role to conflict, which the study attributes to withdrawal. The digest's own body text gets this right, so the framing contradicts itself.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "Across 15 countries, conflict is the most central symptom of compulsive internet use in young people." Why it matters: "…converges on interpersonal symptoms rather than time online, with withdrawal forming the strongest link to psychological distress."

**Issue B. "Teen" for a 15–24 sample** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "teen mental health"
- **Abstract says:** "6204 participants aged 15-24 years."
- **Problem:** Over half the age band are young adults, not teenagers.
- **Suggested fix:** "young people's mental health" (as the body text correctly says).

---

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | Copying a smoker's body language | ⚠️ Minor | "Confederate" not in abstract; NS fit 7 with no reported N — suggest 6 |
| 2 | Quitting sugar / withdrawal symptoms | ⚠️ Minor + 1 Moderate | High symptom-burden group ≠ withdrawal profile; "8pm" invented; two predictors dropped; NS fit → 6 |
| 3 | Heroin abstainers' brains fail to sync | ⚠️ Minor | "First hyperscanning study" and China recruitment site unverifiable |
| 4 | Four in five card packs | ⚠️ Moderate | "Any individual card" should be "every individual card" |
| 5 | Teenage gambling falling but rising in gamers | ⚠️ Minor | OR 3.71 is nearly quadruple, not triple; "rather than traditional routes" added |
| 6 | Short videos cut/raise depression | ⚠️ Moderate | Causal headline contradicts digest's own caveat on cross-sectional SEM |
| 7 | Thirteen years of forced treatment | ⚠️ Moderate | "Most people relapse" — actual figure is 48%; "a" not "the" substance of concern |
| 8 | Maladaptive daydreaming in students | ✅ Accurate | Cleared |
| 9 | Nicotine pouches rated most favourably | ⚠️ Minor | "Fastest-moving in Europe" claim needs external sourcing |
| 10 | Self-regulation backfire | ⚠️ Moderate | "Makes worse" contradicts the pitch's own correlational instruction; 169 was a subsample |
| 11 | Teen self-harm remission | ✅ Accurate | Cleared |
| 12 | Smoking and postpartum depression | ⚠️ Minor | Headline drops confounding hedge; "new mechanism" tag for in silico work |
| 13 | Withdrawal, autistic traits and gaming | ⚠️ Moderate | Mediation applied to outcomes it wasn't tested on; "explains" vs partial mediation |
| 14 | Two kinds of impulsivity in CUD | ⚠️ Minor | "Overturns prior research" wrong; "separate" vs "partially dissociable" |
| 15 | Anxious ultramarathoners | ⚠️ Minor | Mileage-vs-anxiety comparison unverifiable; causal headline on recalled injury |
| 16 | Exercise addiction vs eating disorders | ⚠️ Minor | "Come from" implies origin; authors call findings preliminary |
| 17 | Love addiction and emotional control | ⚠️ Moderate | Structural invariance misread as evidence about gender prevalence |
| 18 | Generative AI and creativity | ⚠️ Moderate | "Until tolerance sets in" implies a trajectory from cross-sectional data |
| 19 | Conflict as hub across 15 countries | ⚠️ Moderate | Most central domain (conflict) conflated with strongest bridge (withdrawal); "teen" for 15–24 |

**Total issues:** 31 (22 Minor, 9 Moderate, 0 Major)
**Entries requiring revision:** 17
**Entries cleared:** 2

**General note:** Contributor first names given in pitch angles (Wojciech Kulesza, Hongjun Duan, Rui Jing, Xin Li, Xiaoping Deng, Yuanyuan Wang) are not verifiable from PubMed abstracts, which give initials only. Surnames and institutions check out in every case; confirm given names before any pitch goes out.
